clue.text: Under orders to come in on what day? It may be Frimley Green's call

definitions.text: It may be Frimley Green's call

indicators.note: the scrambled letters are told to come in, so they go inside the other pieces

parts.note: taken as written
eh? is a puzzled way of saying what?

indicators.note: orders works as a verb here: the word Under is put in a new order

explanation.surface: Someone under orders asks which day they must report for duty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'orders' rearranges the first word and 'to come in' puts it inside the rest. Frimley Green, in Surrey, hosted the Lakeside world darts championship, where a ton scored is called out.
explanation.definitionFit: A darts referee calls out each score, and a ton is a common shout at the oche.

clue.text: Noisy celebratory free-for-all — time to grab a drink!

indicators.note: to grab means the pieces close round the next letter
noisy means the word is taken by how it sounds rather than how it is spelt

parts.note: an orgy is a wild party, a free-for-all of revelry

explanation.surface: A rowdy party breaks out: time to seize a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: ORGE is a sound-alike of ORGY; 'to grab' puts A between it and T.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweet syrup flavoured with almonds and orange-flower water, diluted to make a cordial.

clue.text: This'll do for one — and three noughts!

indicators.note: and here joins the definition to the words that contain the letters in their middle

explanation.surface: A claim that one is sufficient, alongside three zeroes.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits across 'three noughts'.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying this declares the amount sufficient, as when someone has had plenty.

clue.text: Not a chip off 'this' old block roaming peninsular belt!

definitions.text: Not a chip off 'this' old block

indicators.note: roaming means wandering about, so these letters move around

explanation.surface: No mere copy of the father, wandering a coastal strip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'roaming' rearranges PENINSULAR BELT.
explanation.definitionFit: A block that cannot shatter into shards will never yield a chip, playing on the idiom for a child like its parent.

clue.text: Puzzle Editor's in muddle!

indicators.note: muddle means jumble up, so these letters are mixed

explanation.surface: A crossword editor finds themself confused.
explanation.walkthrough: 'muddle' rearranges EDITORS IN.
explanation.definitionFit: To bewilder or confuse someone, making them lose their bearings, is to puzzle them.

clue.text: Play + Film = Uranium — Aluminium

indicators.note: the minus sign takes one symbol away while the other takes its place

parts.note: the sign is read as the word equals
Al is the chemical symbol for aluminium
U is the chemical symbol for uranium

explanation.surface: A chemical equation written with sums and elements.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the equals sign as EQUALS, then swap its AL for U.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter Shaffer's drama about a boy who blinds horses was staged and later filmed with Richard Burton.

clue.text: Boundary of backward old city

indicators.note: backward tells us the little word of is read from right to left

parts.note: Ur was an ancient city of Mesopotamia

explanation.surface: A wall marking the limit of some ruined ancient settlement.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a boundary is a shot reaching the rope after bouncing, scoring four runs.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket, a boundary struck along the ground is worth this many runs, so the shot itself is named by the score.

clue.text: They're known by expert to include just over 3 views

indicators.note: to include means the bulbs hold the number inside them

parts.note: an expert knows their onions, a British idiom for being well informed
pi is about 3.14, just over three

explanation.surface: Judgements an expert holds, slightly more than three of them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knows one's onions' is British for knowing a subject thoroughly.
explanation.definitionFit: Opinions and views are synonyms, both meaning what someone thinks.

clue.text: Road orbiting Cinque Port clips motorway with a recurrent pattern

indicators.note: orbiting means going round, so the road abbreviation encircles the rest
clips means holds in a clip, so the port wraps round the motorway

parts.note: Hythe in Kent is one of the Cinque Ports
M is the abbreviation for motorway, as in M1

explanation.surface: A road circling a Kent town grazes the motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: The Cinque Ports are a historic group of English Channel towns in Kent and Sussex; Hythe is one.
explanation.definitionFit: Something given a regular beat or cadence has a repeating pattern of stresses.

clue.text: Up gear here, describing junky?

indicators.note: junky means rubbishy and jumbled, so these letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: Describing an addict who keeps his kit on a high shelf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'junky' rearranges HERE DESCRIBING. 'Up' means mounted on a horse.
explanation.definitionFit: A rider who is up in the saddle wears these trousers, close-fitting below the knee.

clue.text: Total class 14 17 = 1ac and 22 6?

parts.note: filling in the cross-references, the clue says a whole class scores an intelligence quotient of one hundred and forty-four; twelve dozen, 144, and an IQ is a measure of brains, so the clue mocks foolishness by naming its opposite as a number

explanation.surface: A sum totting up a class's combined test scores.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 14 as INTELLIGENCE, 17 as QUOTIENT, 1ac as ONE HUNDRED, 22 as FORTY and 6 as FOUR: 144 is a gross, and IQ wittily stands in for its opposite.
explanation.definitionFit: Gross means flagrant or utter, so the phrase describes blatant foolishness, while gross as a count is 144.

clue.text: See 10
Lean and bony antelope turns head in near-terror

indicators.note: in places the antelope inside the shortened word for terror
near means almost, so the word for terror loses its final letter

parts.note: alarm is sudden fear

indicators.note: the head of the antelope turns over, so its first two letters change places

parts.note: a gnu is an African antelope, the wildebeest

explanation.surface: A thin antelope swings its head round in near-panic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turns head' swaps the antelope's first two letters; 'near' drops the last letter of the word for terror.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone angular has sharp corners showing, being thin with prominent bones.

clue.text: Piggy dashing around at home

indicators.note: around tells us the word for dashing wraps round the word for at home

parts.note: swish means smart and stylish, like dashing
in means at home, as in staying in

explanation.surface: A little pig rushing about the house.
explanation.definitionFit: Both adjectives describe greedy or coarse behaviour likened to that of a hog.

clue.text: Clientele in shambles, divided by 'good' news

indicators.note: divided by means the jumbled letters are split by another piece put inside them
a shambles is a total mess, so the letters of these words are jumbled

explanation.surface: Customers in disarray, split by some pleasing tidings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shambles' rearranges CLIENTELE IN into INTELLIENCE; 'divided by' inserts G among those letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Intelligence in the sense of information or reports, as in military intelligence, is a synonym for news.

clue.text: Elgar now struggling to comprehend Monsieur's language

indicators.note: to comprehend means to take in, so the anagram encloses the abbreviation
struggling suggests things in disorder, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: The setter fails to understand what a Frenchman says.
explanation.walkthrough: 'struggling' rearranges ELGAR NOW; 'to comprehend' puts M inside.
explanation.definitionFit: The Germanic tongue of northern Germany's lowlands is a language distinct from High German.

clue.text: This much in, as Eastern harbours?

definitions.text: This much in, as Eastern harbours?

indicators.note: harbours means holds within, so the answer lies inside these words

explanation.surface: A sailor wonders how much water an Oriental port holds.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits within 'much in, as Eastern'; the whole clue doubles as the definition, being waters that Eastern harbours open on to.
explanation.definitionFit: Ports in the Far East open onto this stretch of the Pacific off the coast of China.

clue.text: Result of division not quite resolved

indicators.note: resolved means broken down and reformed, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A split that has not been fully settled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'resolved' rearranges NOT QUITE.
explanation.definitionFit: Dividing one number by another gives this figure in arithmetic.

clue.text: Domestic manager employs weakling to take a turn in store

indicators.note: in places the two pieces inside the word for store

parts.note: to hoard is to store up
uses means employs

indicators.note: to take a turn tells us the word for weakling is turned round and read backwards

parts.note: a wet is a feeble, ineffectual person in British slang

explanation.surface: A household manager hires a feeble assistant to rotate the stock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to take a turn' reverses WET to TEW. WET is British slang for a feeble, spineless person.
explanation.definitionFit: This servant runs a large household, a domestic manager overseeing staff and supplies.

clue.text: Having to bandage radius: bit pink

indicators.note: having to bandage means wrapping round, so the word for bit encloses the letter

parts.note: a piece is a bit

explanation.surface: A wound to the forearm bone needs dressing: slightly red.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pink' looks like a colour; it is the verb meaning to prick or nick, as with a sword.
explanation.definitionFit: To pink is to stab or puncture lightly, as a fencer does, so it means to perforate.

clue.text: Clue 10 and 11, for starters?

parts.note: the previous long answer, utter foolishness, could be called stupidity in total, while the phrase also names Chinese snacks served as starters

explanation.surface: A hint to begin with the long across answer.
explanation.walkthrough: Dim means stupid and sum means total, so the phrase sums up gross stupidity; it is also a Chinese meal of small dumplings.
explanation.definitionFit: Small Chinese dumplings and snacks are often served first, and the words also gloss total foolishness.

clue.text: Very much like a bigger drink?

definitions.meaning: the British exclamation meaning absolutely, very much so
a pint is twice a half-pint, so a full measure is the opposite of a half

explanation.surface: Keen agreement when offered a larger glass.
explanation.walkthrough: In British pubs beer comes in pints or halves; 'not half!' is British slang for 'yes, very much'.
explanation.definitionFit: The British slang exclamation means emphatically yes, while literally a full pint is the opposite of a smaller glass.

clue.text: When life begins to assume an (alphabetical?) order

definitions.text: When life begins to assume an (alphabetical?) order

parts.words: When life begins to assume an (alphabetical?) order
parts.note: life is said to begin at a certain age, and that number's letters happen to run in alphabetical sequence

explanation.surface: The point at which existence starts to become organised.
explanation.walkthrough: The saying is 'life begins at forty'; its letters F, O, R, T, Y run in alphabetical order.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb names this age as the start of real living, and the word is spelt in alphabetical letters.

clue.text: This writer exhausts himself running over old professors

indicators.note: running over suggests rolling back, so the whole phrase is read backwards

parts.note: this writer is the setter speaking of himself, I
to tire is to exhaust
the setter referring to himself is me

explanation.surface: A writer wears himself out jogging past retired dons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'running over' reverses I TIRE ME, giving the Latin plural.
explanation.definitionFit: Retired academics who keep their title honorifically are emeritus, with this Latin plural for several of them.

clue.text: Avenger catches Liberal with odd instrument

indicators.note: catches means the Avenger's name holds the next letter inside it

parts.note: John Steed was the hero of the British TV series The Avengers
rum is British slang for odd or strange

explanation.surface: A superhero apprehends a Liberal politician carrying a strange object.
explanation.walkthrough: The Avengers here is the 1960s British TV spy series, not Marvel; RUM is British for odd.
explanation.definitionFit: A Caribbean percussion instrument made from an oil barrel, tuned to play melodies.

clue.text: 'Charters' very well-defined

definitions.meaning: to charter a boat or plane is to rent it
high resolution, of an image with lots of detail

explanation.definitionFit: Charters and rents are synonyms as verbs, while split two-and-three the letters give the short form of high resolution.

clue.text: Sporadic hothead rejected this early payment

indicators.note: rejected means thrown back, so the volcano's name is read backwards

parts.note: Etna, the Sicilian volcano, erupts now and then: a fiery head that blows its top intermittently

explanation.surface: A volatile person spurned an advance on their wages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sporadic hothead' looks like a temperamental person; it is an intermittently erupting volcano.
explanation.definitionFit: In poker the stake each player puts up before the deal is paid in advance of play.

clue.text: Pine, maybe, for return from reps on my grievance cases

indicators.note: return means the letters taken are read the other way
the outer words act as cases holding the letters inside them

explanation.surface: Someone longs for a reply about a complaint they lodged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pine' looks like a verb meaning yearn; it is the tree. 'cases' picks MREPSONMYG from the middle, and 'return' reverses it.
explanation.definitionFit: Pines are conifers, an example of the seed plants whose seeds are not enclosed in an ovary.
